In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿About what do they question one another?﴾ ﴿About the great news,﴾ ﴿concerning which they are in disagreement.﴾ Concerning this there are several issues:

First issue: ʿamma (ʿamma, "about what"): its origin is the preposition ʿan (ʿan, "about") joined with the interrogative mā (mā, "what"). Ḥassān (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

ʿalā mā qāma yashtumunī laʾīmun / kakhinzīrin tamarragha fī ramādi
("Upon what did the base wretch rise to revile me, like a pig rolling in ash?")

The common usage is with elision, while the original form is rare. The scholars mentioned several reasons for the elision:

One: al-Zajjaj said: because the mīm shares the nasalization with the alif, so the two became like two identical letters.

Two: al-Jurjani said: when they put mā in an interrogative sense, they dropped its alif to distinguish it from when it is a noun, as in their saying: fīma, bima, lima, ʿalāma, ḥattāma.

Three: they said: the alif was dropped because mā is joined to the preposition so closely that it became like a part of it, to indicate the strength of the connection.

Four: the reason for this elision is lightness in speech, for it is a word very frequently used on the tongue.

Second issue: His words ﴿about what do they question one another?﴾ indicate a question, and His words ﴿about the great news﴾ are the answer to the questioner, and the one who answers is Allah, the Exalted. This indicates His knowledge of the Unseen, indeed of all that is known. If it is said: what is the benefit of mentioning the answer along with it? We say: because presenting speech in the form of question and answer is closer to making it understood and clear. A parallel to this is: ﴿To whom belongs dominion this Day? To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir: 16].

Third issue: ʿIkrima and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read ʿammā (with alif), which is the original form. On the authority of Ibn Kathīr, he read ʿammah with the silent hāʾ (hāʾ al-sakt). Either he treats the connected reading as if it were a pause, or he pauses and begins with ﴿they question one another﴾ ﴿about the great news﴾, supposing an implied verb "they question one another" because what follows explains it, like an ambiguous thing that is then explained.

Fourth issue: mā is a word laid down to seek the quiddities and realities of things. You say: What is kingship? What is the soul? What are the jinn? The intent is to seek their quiddities and explain their realities, and that requires that the sought-after thing be unknown. Then, a great thing which, because of its greatness and the magnitude of its rank, overwhelms the intellect so that it cannot encompass its essence, remains unknown. Thus there is a resemblance between the thing sought with the word mā and the great thing in this respect, and resemblance is one of the causes of metaphor. By this way, mā was made a sign of the greatness of the state of that sought-after thing and the loftiness of its rank. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjīn is?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 8], ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾ [al-Balad: 12]. And you say: Zayd, and what Zayd is!

Fifth issue: tasāʾul (mutual questioning) is that some ask others, like the reciprocal form, and it may also be used in the sense of discussing it, even if there is no question from some to others. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they turn to one another, questioning﴾ ﴿One of them says, "I had a companion"﴾ ﴿who used to say, "Are you indeed among those who affirm?"﴾. This indicates the meaning of talking, so the sense of the speech is "about what do they talk to one another?" This is the view of al-Farrāʾ.

Sixth issue: Regarding who those were who used to question one another, there are possibilities. One: they are the disbelievers, and the evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿No! They will come to know.﴾ ﴿Again, no! They will come to know.﴾ The pronoun in (yatasāʾalūn), (hum fīhi mukhtalifūn), and (sa-yaʿlamūn) refers to one thing. And His saying ﴿No! They will come to know﴾ is a threat, and threat befits only the disbelievers. Thus it is established that the pronoun in His saying ﴿they question one another﴾ refers to the disbelievers. If it is said: what do you make of His saying ﴿concerning which they are in disagreement﴾, given that the disbelievers were in agreement in denying the Resurrection? We say: we do not concede that they were in agreement in denying the Resurrection. That is because among them were those who affirmed a spiritual return, and they are the majority of the Christians. As for the bodily return, among them were those who doubted it, as in His saying: ﴿I do not think the Hour will ever come; and even if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have a better place with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. Among them were those who insisted on denial, saying: ﴿There is only our life of this world; we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected﴾ [al-Muminun: 37]. Among them were those who acknowledged it but denied the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. So their disagreement about it did occur. Moreover, even supposing they were all deniers, perhaps they differed in the manner of their denial. Some denied it because they denied the Maker, the Chooser; others denied it because they believed that the re-creation of what has ceased to exist is impossible in its very essence, and the capable Chooser is capable only of what is possible in itself. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿concerning which they are in disagreement﴾.

The second possibility: those who used to question one another were both the disbelievers and the believers, and they all used to question about it. As for the Muslim, it is so that he may gain more insight and certainty in his religion; as for the disbeliever, it is by way of mockery, or by way of raising doubts and dubious objections.

The third possibility: they used to question the Messenger, saying: what is this that you threaten us with concerning the matter of the Hereafter?

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿About the great news﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: The exegetes mentioned three aspects in the interpretation of "the great news":

One: that it is the Resurrection, and this is the closest view, and it is indicated by several things:

One: His saying "they will come to know". The apparent meaning is that they will come to know this about which they question one another at a time when that knowledge will not benefit them, and it is known that this is the Resurrection.

Two: He, exalted is He, showed His capacity over all possibilities by His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting place?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿the Day the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-Naba': 18].

This requires that He, exalted is He, only put forward this premise to demonstrate His capacity to establish the Resurrection. Since the matter which Allah, exalted is He, established by rational proof in this surah is this matter, it is established that the great news about which they were questioning is the Day of Resurrection.

Three: that "the Great" is a name for this Day, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected﴾ ﴿for a tremendous Day﴾ ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 4–6], and His saying: ﴿Say: It is a great news﴾ ﴿from which you turn away﴾ [Sad: 67–68]. And because this Day is the greatest of things, for it is the ultimate of the terror and fear of creation from it, so it was fitting to specify the name "the Great" for it.

The first: that the great news is that about which they used to differ, and that is the Qur'an, for some of them called it sorcery, some called it poetry, and some said it is "tales of the ancients". As for the Resurrection and the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, they were in agreement in denying both. This is weak, because we have shown that the disagreement did occur regarding the Resurrection.

The second: that "naba'" is the name of the report, not the name of the thing reported. So explaining "naba'" as the Qur'an is preferable to explaining it as the Resurrection or prophethood, because that in itself is not a "naba'" but something reported. What strengthens this is that the Qur'an is called "reminder" (dhikr), "admonition" (tadhkira), "reminder" (dhikra), "guidance" (hidaya), and "discourse" (hadith), so the name "naba'" is more fitting for it than for the Resurrection and prophethood. The answer to this: if the name "naba'" is more fitting for these expressions, then the name "the Great" is more fitting for the Resurrection and for prophethood, because there is no greatness in words; greatness is only in meanings. The first party may say that it is great also in eloquence and in containing many sciences. It may be answered that "great" is literally applied to bodies and metaphorically to other things. And once the contradiction is established, the evidences we mentioned remain sound.

The third view: that the great news is the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. They said: when the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, was sent, they began to question one another: what is this that has happened? So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿About what do they question one another?﴾. This is because they were astonished that Allah sent Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, to them, as He said: ﴿Rather, they wonder that a warner from among themselves has come to them, and the disbelievers say, "This is an astonishing thing"﴾ [Qaf: 2]. They were also astonished that he brought monotheism, as He said: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing﴾ [Sad: 5]. So Allah, exalted is He, related their mutual questioning out of wonder by His saying: ﴿About what do they question one another?﴾.

Second issue: On how this verse connects with what precedes it, there are several views:

One, which is the view of the Basrans: His saying ﴿About what do they question one another?﴾ is a complete sentence, then He said ﴿About the great news﴾, and the implied meaning is: ﴿They question one another﴾ ﴿about the great news﴾, except that He omitted "they question one another" in the second verse because its occurrence in the first verse indicates it.

Two: that His saying ﴿About the great news﴾ is an interrogative connected to what precedes it, and the implied meaning is: "About what do they question one another about the great news concerning which they are in disagreement?", except that it suffices with the interrogative before it since it is connected to it, and it serves as a translation and clarification of it, as was read in His saying: (When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?) [al-Saffat: 16] with a kasra on the alif without an interrogative, because their denial was only of the resurrection; but since the interrogative appeared at the beginning of the speech, it was limited to it. So it is likewise here.

Three: and this is the choice of the Kufans: that the second verse is connected to the first with the sense of "for what reason do they question one another about the great news?", and ʿamma is in meaning as though it were "for what reason", and this is the view of al-Farrāʾ.

This requires that He, exalted is He, only put forward this premise to demonstrate His capacity to establish the Resurrection. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 78, verses 15–17:**

God's words: ﴿That We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation﴾ ﴿and gardens of entwined foliage﴾. In this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Every plant that grows from the earth either has no stalk or has one. If it has no stalk, it either has husks (*akmam*, sing. *kumm*), which is grain (*habb*), or it has no husks, which is herbage (*hashish*). This is what is meant here by His words "vegetation" (*nabatan*). Both of these categories are referred to in God's words: ﴿Eat, and pasture your livestock﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:54]. As for what has a stalk, it is a tree. When a large quantity of these gather together, it is called a garden (*jannah*). Thus it is established by rational proof that what grows from the earth is confined to these three categories. God mentioned grain first because it is the basis of nourishment. He mentioned vegetation next because all other animals need it. He mentioned gardens last because the need for fruits is not essential.

**The second issue:** Scholars differ regarding *alfafan* (entwined). The author of *al-Kashshaf* mentions that it has no singular, like *al-awza'* and *al-akhyaf*. *Al-awza'* are scattered groups, and *al-akhyaf* are mixed groups. Many lexicographers, however, have affirmed a singular for it, and then they differed about it. Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i said its singular is *liff* with a kasra. Al-Kisa'i added *luff* with a damma. Al-Mubarrad rejected the damma and said rather that its singular is *laffa'* (f. sing.), its plural is *luff*, and the plural of *liff* is *alfaf*. It has also been said that it may be the plural of *lafif*, like *sharif* and *ashraf*; this was transmitted by al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him. Having understood this, we say: God's words ﴿and gardens of *alfafan*﴾ mean "intertwined," and the meaning is that in every garden, the trees within it are gathered together and close to one another. Do you not see that they say "*imra'ah laffa'*" (a woman with thick shins and tightly packed flesh) when she is thick-legged and her flesh is compact, to the degree that her parts cling together due to their closeness?

**The third issue:** Al-Ka'bi was among those who held the doctrine of natural causes (*al-taba'i'*). He argued with God's words ﴿That We may bring forth thereby grain and vegetation﴾, and said that it indicates the falsity of the view of those who say that God does not do anything through the mediation of something else.

God's words: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾.

Know that the nine things God enumerated, considered in terms of their originatedness in their essences and attributes, and considered in terms of their possibility in their essences and attributes, indicate a capable and choosing Agent. Considered in terms of the firm perfection within them, they indicate that their Maker is knowing. Then, that eternal Agent must have necessary knowledge and power, for if they were contingent, He would require another agent, and this would lead to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*), which is impossible. When knowledge and power are necessary, it becomes necessary that they relate to everything that can validly be an object of power and knowledge; otherwise He would require a specifier (*mukhassis*), which is impossible. Since this is so, He must be capable of all possible things and knowing of all knowable things. The possibility has been established, and the universality of power over corporeal beings has been established. Therefore, whatever is valid for one of them is valid for the others. Just as splitting asunder, cleaving, and darkening are valid for the celestial bodies, so they must be valid for the bodies. When possibility is established and the universality of power and knowledge is established, it is established that He, exalted is He, is capable of destroying this world and capable of bringing into being another world. At that point it is established that the claim of the Resurrection is rationally possible. Up to this point, it can be established by reason. As for what lies beyond that, such as the time of its occurrence and the manner of its occurrence, there is no path to it except through revelation (*al-sam'*).

Then, He, exalted is He, spoke about these matters in His words ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned some of the conditions of the Resurrection. The first of them is His words ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾. The meaning is that this day was, in God's decree and judgment, a limit by which the world is timed, or a limit to which all creatures come, or it was an appointed time for what God promised of reward and punishment, or it was an appointed time for the gathering of all creatures for the decision of judgments and the settling of disputes.

God's words: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾.

Know that the nine things God enumerated, considered in terms of their originatedness in their essences and attributes, and considered in terms of their possibility in their essences and attributes, indicate a capable and choosing Agent. Considered in terms of the firm perfection within them, they indicate that their Maker is knowing. Then, that eternal Agent must have necessary knowledge and power, for if they were contingent, He would require another agent, and this would lead to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*), which is impossible. When knowledge and power are necessary, it becomes necessary that they relate to everything that can validly be an object of power and knowledge; otherwise He would require a specifier (*mukhassis*), which is impossible. Since this is so, He must be capable of all possible things and knowing of all knowable things. The possibility has been established, and the universality of power over corporeal beings has been established. Therefore, whatever is valid for one of them is valid for the others. Just as splitting asunder, cleaving, and darkening are valid for the celestial bodies, so they must be valid for the bodies. When possibility is established and the universality of power and knowledge is established, it is established that He, exalted is He, is capable of destroying this world and capable of bringing into being another world. At that point it is established that the claim of the Resurrection is rationally possible. Up to this point, it can be established by reason. As for what lies beyond that, such as the time of its occurrence and the manner of its occurrence, there is no path to it except through revelation (*al-sam'*).

Then, He, exalted is He, spoke about these matters in His words ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned some of the conditions of the Resurrection. The first of them is His words ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾. The meaning is that this day was, in God's decree and judgment, a limit by which the world is timed, or a limit to which all creatures come, or it was an appointed time for what God promised of reward and punishment, or it was an appointed time for the gathering of all creatures for the decision of judgments and the settling of disputes.

Third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the sky will be opened, and it will become gates﴾.

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read فُتِحَتِ (*futihat*, "was opened") with a light (unstressed) form, while the rest read it with the emphatic form (*tathqīl*, doubled consonant). The meaning is: its opened gates become numerous, for the descent of the angels. Al-Qāḍī said: "This opening is the meaning of His saying: ﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 1], and ﴿When the sky is cleft asunder﴾ [al-Infitar: 1], since opening, splitting and cleaving are close in meaning." I say: this is not strong, because what is understood from the opening of a gate is not what is understood from splitting and cleaving. It may be that the sky becomes gates, and then those gates are opened, even though no splitting or cleaving occurs in the body of the sky. Rather, the textual proofs indicate that when these gates are opened, splitting, cleaving and complete annihilation occur.

If it is said: His saying, ﴿And the sky will be opened, and it will become gates﴾ indicates that the sky in its entirety becomes gates, so how can that be conceived? We say: there are several explanations:

The first: those gates, because they are so numerous, become as if they were nothing but opened gates, like His saying: ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], meaning, as if all of it had become springs gushing forth.

The second: al-Wahidi said: this is from the category of omitting a modified noun, and the implied meaning is: "it became possessed of gates" (*dhāt abwāb*).

The third: the pronoun in His saying ﴿and it became gates﴾ refers back to an implied element, and the meaning is: those open places became gates for the descent of the angels, just as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22].

Fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾.

Know that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the states of these mountains in various places in His Book in different ways, and it is possible to reconcile them in the manner we state. Their first state is crumbling, which is His saying: ﴿And the earth and the mountains will be lifted and crushed with a single crushing﴾ [al-Haqqah: 14].

The second state for them is that they become ﴿like carded wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. Allah mentioned this in His saying: ﴿The day when people will be like scattered moths, and the mountains will be like carded wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 4–5], and His saying: ﴿The day when the sky will be like molten brass, and the mountains will be like wool﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 8–9].

The third state: they become like dust particles, because they are broken into pieces and scattered after having been like carded wool. This is His saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking, and the mountains are crumbled to powder, and become scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4–6].

The fourth state: they are blown away, because they, along with the preceding states, remain fixed in their places while the earth beneath them is not exposed; so they are blown off from it by sending winds upon them. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord will scatter them with a scattering﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105].

The fifth state: the winds lift them from the surface of the earth and scatter them as particles in the air, as if they were dust. Whoever looks at them from a distance thinks they are solid bodies because of their density, while in reality they are moving; but their movement, caused by the passing of the winds through them, makes them dispersed and crumbling. This is His saying: ﴿And you will see them, and they will pass like the passing of clouds﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Then He explained that this motion occurs by His subjugation and command, so He said: ﴿And on the day We set the mountains in motion, you will see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47].

The sixth state: they become a mirage, meaning nothing. Whoever looks at their places will find nothing in them, just as whoever sees a mirage from a distance, when he reaches the place where he saw it, finds nothing there. And Allah knows best.

Know that the states mentioned up to this point are general states. From here He describes the terrors of Hell and its conditions.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 78, verse 21:

Among these, first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying in wait﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn Ya'mur read (أنّ جهنم) with a fat-ha on the hamzah (inna, "that"), giving the sense of a causal clause explaining the establishment of the Hour: because Hell has been a lying in wait for the tyrants. It is as if it were said: it is thus for the establishment of recompense.

The second issue: "has been a lying in wait" means in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. It was also said: "it became" (one). These two opinions were transmitted by al-Qaffal, may Allah have mercy on him. There is a third view on this, mentioned by al-Qadi (al-Baydawi). For when we interpret al-Mirsad (lying in wait) as "one who watches for," it conveys that Hell has been, since ancient times, like one awaiting their arrival and like one who summons and seeks them.

The third issue: Regarding al-Mirsad there are two views. The first: al-Mirsad is a noun for the place where one keeps watch, just as al-Midmar (the training ground) is the place where horses are trained, and al-Minhaj (the path) is the place where one travels. On this view there are two possibilities. The first is that the guardians of Hell watch over the disbelievers. The second is that the passage of the believers and their crossing was over Hell, due to His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ (Maryam 19:71). So the guardians of Paradise meet the believers at Hell and watch over them there.

The second view: al-Mirsad is a form of intensive (mif'al) from al-Rasd (watching, awaiting), meaning that this occurs frequently from it. The mif'al is among the patterns of intensification, like al-Minzar (telescope), al-Mi'mar (one who builds much) and al-Mit'an (one who thrusts much). It was said: it watches over the enemies of Allah and oppresses them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It almost bursts with rage﴾ (al-Mulk 67:8). It was said: it watches over every disbeliever and hypocrite. Those who hold the first view supported their position with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in wait﴾ (al-Fajr 89:14). Had al-Mirsad been an adjective, it would have been necessary to say: "Indeed, your Lord is a mirsad."

The fourth issue: The verse indicates that Hell was created, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been a lying in wait﴾, i.e., prepared. If that is so, Paradise is likewise, because there is no one who makes a distinction.

**[Commentary of al-Razi, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, on Surah 78, verses 22–23]**

Second: His saying ﴿for the transgressors, a destination﴾. There are two possible readings. If we say that Hell is a *mirsad* (a place of lying-in-wait) for the disbelievers only, then His saying *lil-taghin* (﴿for the transgressors﴾) completes the preceding statement, and the sense is: "Indeed Hell was a *mirsad* for the transgressors." Then His saying *ma'aban* (﴿a destination﴾) is a *badal* (substitute, or appositive) for *mirsadan* (﴿a lying-in-wait﴾). If we say that it was a *mirsad* absolutely, for both the disbelievers and the believers, then His saying ﴿Indeed Hell has been a lying-in-wait﴾ is a complete statement, and His saying ﴿for the transgressors, a destination﴾ is an independent sentence (*mubtada'*), as if it were said: "Indeed Hell is a lying-in-wait for all, and a destination for the transgressors in particular." Whoever adopts the first view does not pause at *mirsadan*. Whoever adopts the second view pauses there, and then says: the intended meaning of "the transgressors" is those who were arrogant towards their Lord and exceeded bounds in opposing and contesting Him. His saying *ma'aban* means a place of return, that is, a final destination and abode.

Third: His saying ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾. Know that when He, the Exalted, explained that Hell is a destination for the transgressors, and explained the duration of their stay there, He said: ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾. Here there are several issues.

The first issue: al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) recite *labithin* (لابِثِينَ), while Hamzah recites *labithin* (لَبِثِينَ). On this there are two views. Al-Farra' said: they have one meaning; it is said *labith* and *labith*, like *ta'mi'* and *tama'*, and *farih* and *farih*, and this is common. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *al-labith* is stronger, because the *labith* is one from whom staying has been found, and one is not called *labith* except someone whose nature is staying, which is to settle in a place and hardly ever depart from it.

The second issue: al-Farra' said: the original root of *hiqab* lies in succession and consecutiveness. It is said *ahqaba* when one follows up (*ardafa*), and from it comes *haqibah* (a saddle-bag or pouch), and from it, "whoever carries a burden has *ihtaqaba*." So according to this meaning, ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾ means: remaining therein for consecutive eras, one following another. This is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I journey on for a long age﴾ [al-Kahf: 60], which may mean consecutive years until I reach it or become familiar. Know that the word *ahqab* has as its singular *huqb*, which according to the lexicographers is eighty years. *Hiqab* (plural of *huqb*) means years, and its singular is *hiqbah*, which is a period of time from the ages with no fixed term. Then several views have been reported from the exegetes concerning it:

The first: 'Ata', al-Kalbi and Muqatil reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying *ahqaban* (﴿ages﴾), that one *huqb* is some eighty-odd years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is a thousand years of the days of this world. Ibn 'Umar narrated something similar, as a *marfu'* report (one traced back to the Prophet ﷺ).

The second: Hilal al-Hajari asked 'Ali (peace be upon him), and he said: a *huqb* is a hundred years, a year is twelve months, a month is thirty days, and a day is a thousand years.

The third: al-Hasan said: no one knows what the *ahqab* are, but one *huqb* is seventy thousand years, a day of which is like a thousand years of what you count.

(If it is said): His saying *ahqaban* (ages), however long they are, is still finite, whereas the punishment of the people of the Fire is not finite. Indeed, had He said *labithina fiha al-ahqab* (remaining therein for the ages), this question would not arise. A parallel to this question is His saying concerning the people of the *qiblah* (the believers): ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud: 107]. We say: the answer is in several respects.

The first: the word *ahqab* does not indicate the passing of an *huqb* that has an end. Rather, each single *huqb* is finite, and the meaning is that they remain therein for ages; whenever one *huqb* passes, another *huqb* follows it, and so on forever.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that they remain therein for ages, during which they taste neither coolness nor drink. These ages are a time-limit for one kind of punishment, namely that they taste neither coolness nor drink except boiling water (*hamim*) and dark, pus-like liquid (*ghassaq*). Then after the ages, they are exchanged from the *hamim* and the *ghassaq* for another kind of punishment.

The third: suppose His saying *ahqaban* implies finiteness; still, the indication of their leaving is an indication by implication (*mafhum*), whereas the explicit statement (*mantuq*) shows that they will not leave. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not come out of it, and theirs is a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 37].

When you understand the interpretation we have mentioned, it becomes clear that God has shown that they had reached such a degree of baseness and corruption that it is rationally impossible for anything worse to exist. Since their deeds were thus, the fitting recompense for them is a great punishment. Thereby the correctness of what He stated earlier in His saying: ﴿a fitting recompense﴾ is established. How great are the subtleties of the Qur'an, although these great cycles have continued and no one has noticed them! Praise be to God with a praise befitting the loftiness of His station and the clarity of His proof, for having singled out this weak servant with knowledge of these secrets.

Know that the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿And they denied Our signs with (full) denial﴾ indicates that they denied all of God's proofs concerning monotheism (tawhid), prophethood (nubuwwa), the return (ma'ad), the laws (shara'i') and the Qur'an. This indicates the full condition of the theoretical power in baseness, corruption, and distance from the right path. His saying "kiddaban" (with full denial) means "takdhiban" (denial). It is a fi'al form of the verbal nouns of the tafa''ul pattern. Al-Zajjaj recited:

"Indeed, you have long delayed me from my companions and from needs whose fulfilment is from our healing."

From qadaytu qidha'an (I fulfilled a need). Al-Farra' said: this is an eloquent Yemeni dialect. Its parallel is kharraqtu al-qamisa kharraqan (I tore the shirt into tears). An Arab of them said to me at al-Marwa, asking my opinion: "Is shaving (al-halq) more beloved to you or trimming (al-qiṣṣar)?" The author of al-Kashshaf said: "I was explaining a verse, and some of them said: 'You have explained it with a fissar (explanation) never heard of.'" It was also read with the light pronunciation (takhfif), and in it there are several aspects:

First: it is a verbal noun of kadhdhaba (to deny), as evidenced by his saying:

"So I believed her, or I denied her, and a man benefits from his lying."

This is like His saying: ﴿And God made you grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17], meaning: "they denied Our signs, so they denied with denial."

Second: that it be in the accusative governed by "kadhdhabu" (they denied), because it includes the meaning of kadhdhabu, since every one who denies the truth is a liar.

Third: that kidhdhab be taken in the sense of mukadhaba (mutual denial). Its meaning is: "they denied Our signs, so they engaged in mutual denial," or "they denied them while being liars," since when they were liars in the sight of the Muslims, and the Muslims were liars in their sight, there was mutual denial between them. It was also read as such, being the plural of kadhib (kadhibin), meaning: "they denied Our signs being liars." The kadhdhab may also mean the singular intensive form, one who is eloquent in lying, as one says: "a man kadhdhab," like your saying hassan and bakhkhal. It is then made an adjective of the verbal noun of kadhdhabu, meaning "a denial, intensely lying in its falsehood."

Know that when He, exalted be He, had explained that the corruption of their state, both in the practical faculty and in the theoretical faculty, had reached its utmost limits and greatest extremes, He then explained that the details of those states, in their quantity and their quality, are known to Him, and the measure of punishment they deserve is known to Him. So He said: ﴿And all things We have enumerated in a Book﴾. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Zajjaj said: "kull" (all) is in the accusative, governed by a verb implied and explained by "ahsaynahu" (We have enumerated it), and the meaning is: "And We have enumerated every thing." Abu al-Sammal read "wa-kullu" with the nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence.

The second issue: His saying ﴿And all things We have enumerated﴾ means: We have known every thing with a knowledge that does not cease and does not change. Its parallel is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Allah has enumerated it, and they have forgotten it﴾ [al-Mujadila: 6]. Know that this verse indicates that He, exalted be He, is knowing of the particulars (al-juz'iyyat). Know also that a verse like this does not admit of interpretation (ta'wil), because He, exalted be He, mentioned this as confirmation of what He had claimed in His saying: ﴿a recompense in accordance [with their deeds]﴾. It is as if He, exalted be He, were saying: I know all that they did, and I know the aspects of those actions, their states and their considerations, by which the deservingness of reward and punishment is established. Therefore, I do not inflict upon them any punishment except the amount that is commensurate with their deeds. It is well known that this amount is accomplished only if it is established that He, exalted be He, knows the particulars. And once this is established, it becomes clear that whoever denies it is definitely a disbeliever.

The third issue: His saying ﴿We have enumerated it in a Book﴾ has two aspects:

The first: its estimate is "We have enumerated it with an enumeration" (ihsa'an). He turned from that word to this word because writing (al-kitaba) is the ultimate in the strength of knowledge. For this reason the Prophet, upon him be peace, said: "Bind knowledge by writing it down." So it is as if He, exalted be He, said: "And all things We have enumerated with an enumeration equal in strength, firmness and affirmation to the written." Thus the purpose of His saying "a Book" is the emphasis of that enumeration and knowledge. Know that this emphasis came according to what befits the understanding of the people of the outward meaning, for what is written is subject to cessation, whereas God's knowledge of things is not subject to cessation, because it is necessary by His very essence.

The second opinion: His saying "a Book" is a circumstantial clause (hal) in the sense of "written," and the meaning is: "And all things We have enumerated while they are written in the Preserved Tablet," like His saying: ﴿And all things We have enumerated in a clear Imam﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12], or in the scrolls of the recording angels.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 78, verse 30:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So taste; for We shall not increase you except in punishment.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, first described the states of punishment, then asserted that it was ﴿a fitting recompense﴾, then explained the details of their vile deeds, and it became clear that what He had asserted at first, that this punishment was ﴿a fitting recompense﴾, was true, he therefore repeated the mention of the punishment. His saying "So taste" with the fa' (fa, the particle of consequence, indicating) that it is a recompense, draws attention to the fact that the command to taste is motivated by the vile deeds whose description has preceded. Thus this fa' conveys the very same benefit as His saying ﴿a fitting recompense﴾.

The fourth issue: this verse indicates intensification in the punishment in several respects.

The first: His saying ﴿for We shall not increase you﴾, and the word lan (never) is for emphasis in negation.

The second: in His saying ﴿they used not to hope for a reckoning﴾ He mentioned them in the third person, and in His saying "So taste" He addressed them directly, and this indicates complete wrath.

The third: He enumerated the forms of punishment, then judged that it was a recompense corresponding to their deeds, then enumerated their disgraceful acts, then said "So taste," as if He had issued a ruling and established the proofs, then repeated that same ruling exactly, and this indicates intensification in punishment. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This verse is the most severe in the Qur'an for the people of the Fire: whenever they seek relief from one kind of punishment, they are given relief with something more severe than it."

There remain two questions regarding the verse.

The first question: Did He not say, describing the disbelievers: ﴿Allah will neither speak to them nor look at them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77]? So here, when He said to them "So taste," has He not spoken to them? The answer: most of the exegetes said the sense of the verse is: it will be said to them, "So taste." One may object: on this interpretation, it is not fitting for that speaker to say ﴿for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾; rather this speech is fitting only for Allah. The closer answer is that one says: His saying ﴿nor speak to them﴾ means He will not speak to them with good, beneficial speech, for the specification of a general statement is not far-fetched, especially when there is an indicator, since His saying ﴿nor speak to them﴾ was mentioned only to show that He will not benefit them nor give them any weight, and that is achieved only through good speech.

The second question: This verse indicates that He, exalted is He, increases the punishment of the disbeliever forever. That increase is either deserved by them or not deserved. If it is deserved by them, then leaving it out at the beginning was a favour, and a generous one who has waived his right is not fitting to take it back afterward. And if that increase is not deserved, then bringing it upon them is injustice, and that is impermissible for Allah. The answer: just as a thing has an effect according to the property of its essence, so likewise when it lasts, its effect increases according to that duration. Therefore, the longer the duration, the greater the pain. Also, that increase is deserved, and leaving it out at some times does not necessitate acquittal or remission. And Allah knows best what He intended.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the threat against the disbelievers, He followed it with the promise to the righteous, which consists of several matters:

**Page [20]**

The first point: His saying, ﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing is a place of triumph﴾. As for the God-fearing (*muttaqi*), its tafsir (interpretation) has been explained in many places earlier. *Mafazan* may be a verbal noun meaning triumph and attainment of the desired aim, or it may denote a place of triumph. Triumph may mean success in attaining what is desired, or success in being saved from punishment, or both together. In my view, interpreting it as success in attaining what is desired is preferable to interpreting it as success in being saved from punishment, and preferable to interpreting it as both together, meaning salvation from destruction and arrival at what is desired. This is because God explained *mafaz* by what follows it, His saying, ﴿gardens and vineyards﴾, so it is necessary that *mafaz* refers only to this. If it is said: "Deliverance from destruction is more important than obtaining pleasure, so why was the more important omitted and the less important mentioned?" We reply: deliverance from destruction does not necessarily entail winning pleasure and good, whereas winning pleasure and good necessarily entails deliverance from destruction. Therefore, mentioning the latter is more appropriate.

The second point: His saying, ﴿gardens and vineyards﴾. *Hada'iq* is the plural of *hadiqah*, which is an orchard enclosed by a wall, from their saying "they encircled him" (*ahdaqu bihi*), meaning they surrounded him. The indefiniteness in His saying "*a'nabạn*" (vineyards) indicates the grandeur of the state of those vineyards.

The third point: His saying, ﴿and maidens of equal age﴾. *Kawa'ib* is the plural of *ka'ib*, which refers to young women whose breasts have become firm and rounded, meaning the breast is prominent like an ankle-bone and a sphere.

The fourth point: His saying, ﴿and a cup overflowing﴾. Regarding *dihaq* there are several opinions. The first, which is the view of most lexicographers such as Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Zajjaj, al-Kisa'i and al-Mubarrad, is that *dihaqan* means filled to the brim. Ibn 'Abbas called a slave of his and said: "Give us *dihaqan*," and the slave brought it full, and Ibn 'Abbas said: "This is *dihaq*." 'Ikrimah said: "I often heard Ibn 'Abbas say: 'Give us to drink and fill it up for us.'" The second opinion: *dihaqan* means consecutive, which is the view of Abu Hurayrah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. al-Wahidi said: The origin of this view is from the Arabs' saying *iddahaqat al-hijaratu idhaqan*, meaning the stones pressed tightly together and some of them entered into others. al-Layth mentioned it, and the consecutive is like the interlocking. The third opinion: it is narrated from 'Ikrimah that he said: *dihaqan* means pure. According to this view, *dihaq* may be the plural of *dahiq*, which is two pieces of wood by which something is pressed. The intended meaning of "cup" is wine. al-Dahhak said: "Every cup in the Qur'an is wine." The implied meaning is: "and wine having *dihaq*," that is, pressed and purified with *dihaq*.

[Page 20]

The fifth point: His saying, ﴿They will hear therein no idle talk or lying﴾. There are two questions concerning this verse.

The first question: To what does the pronoun in His saying "*fiha*" (therein) refer? The answer: there are two views. The first is that it refers to the cup, meaning that no idle talk occurs among them over the cup they drink, because people who drink wine in this world speak falsehood, whereas the people of Paradise, when they drink, their intellects are not altered and they do not speak idle talk. The second is that the reference is to Paradise, meaning that they do not hear in Paradise anything they dislike.

The second question: *Kidhdhab* with the doubled letter (*tashdid*) indicates intensification. Its occurrence in His saying, ﴿and they denied Our signs with [great] denial﴾, is appropriate, because it indicates intensification in describing them as liars. But its occurrence here is not fitting, because His saying, ﴿They will hear therein no idle talk or lying﴾, indicates that they do not hear great lying, and this does not negate that they hear little lying. The purpose of the verse is not that, but rather the intensification in negating that they hear lying at all. The conclusion is that this form indicates the negation of intensification, whereas what is fitting for the verse is intensification in negation. The answer: al-Kisa'i read the first with the doubled letter and the second without it, and perhaps his purpose was what we have established in this question, because the reading without the doubled letter here indicates that they do not hear lying at all, since *kidhab* (without doubling) and *kadhib* have the same meaning. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: *kidhab* is the verbal noun of *kadhaba*, like *kitab* is the verbal noun of *kataba*. When this is so, the reading without doubling indicates intensification in negation, while the reading with doubling in the first instance indicates intensification in affirmation. Thus the purpose of this reading is achieved in both places in its most complete form. If we adopt al-Kisa'i's reading, the question is resolved. If we adopt the reading with doubling in both places, which is the reading of the rest, then the excuse for it is that His saying, ﴿They will hear therein no idle talk or lying﴾, refers back to what came before in His saying, ﴿and they denied Our signs with [great] denial﴾. The meaning is that these fortunate people do not hear their confused, false and corrupt speech. The conclusion is that the blessings reaching them will be free from the crowding of their enemies, from hearing their corrupt speech, and from their false and baseless statements.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 78, verse 37:**

Know that when He (exalted is He) had elaborated on the threat against the disbelievers and the promise to the God-fearing, He concluded that discourse with His saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, the Most Merciful. They have no power to address Him.﴾ On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding "Lord of the heavens" and "the Most Merciful," there are three modes of recitation (qira'at). The first is the nominative (raf') in both words, which is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr. The second is the genitive (jarr) in both, which is the reading of 'Asim and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir. The third is the genitive in the first word with the nominative in the second, which is the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. For the nominative there are several possibilities:

The first: "Lord of the heavens" is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), "the Most Merciful" is its predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate), and then a new sentence is begun (isti'naf, resumption): "They have no power to address Him."

The second: "Lord of the heavens" is the subject, "the Most Merciful" is an adjective (sifah), and "they have no power" is the predicate.

The third: the subject is omitted, and the implied meaning is "He is the Lord of the heavens, He is the Most Merciful," and then "they have no power" is begun as a new sentence.

The fourth: "the Most Merciful" and "they have no power" are both predicates.

As for the genitive, it is in apposition (badal) to "your Lord." As for the case of the genitive in the first word and the nominative in the second, the first is in apposition to "your Lord," while the second is nominative because it is a subject whose predicate is "they have no power."

**The second issue:** To whom does the pronoun in His saying "they have no power" refer? There are three opinions on this.

The first: 'Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it refers to the polytheists, meaning that the polytheists will not be addressed, whereas the believers will intercede, and God will accept that from them.

The second: al-Qadi said that it refers to the believers, and the meaning is that the believers have no power to address God regarding any matter, because it has been established that He is just and does not act unjustly. Therefore, it is established that the punishment He inflicted on the disbelievers is just, and that the reward He bestowed on the believers is just, and that He does not diminish their due. So for what reason would they address Him? This view is closer than the first, because what preceded this verse was a mention of the believers, not a mention of the disbelievers.

The third: that it is a pronoun referring to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. This is the correct view, for none of the created beings has the power to address God or speak with Him. As for the intercessions that take place by His permission, they do not apply to this statement, because it denies ownership, and what is obtained by His grace and bounty is not owned. Thus it is established that this question is not compelling.

Rationally, the following considerations show that none of the created beings has the power to address God:

**The first:** Everything other than Him is His possession, and a possession does not have any right over its owner.

**The second:** The meaning of having a right over Him is that if He did not act, He would deserve blame, and if He did act, He would deserve praise. Whoever is like this is deficient in his essence, perfected by something else, and God is exalted above that.

**The third:** He knows the ugliness of ugly acts and knows that He is independent of them. Whoever is such does not commit an ugly act. Whoever is prevented from committing an ugly act, no one has the right to demand anything from him or to say to him, "Why did you do that?" The first two considerations are based on the view of the People of the Sunnah, while the third is based on the view of the Mu'tazilah. Thus it is established that none of the created beings has the power to address its Lord or to demand of its God.

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned that none of creation is able to address God regarding anything or make a demand of Him for anything, He established this meaning and confirmed it, saying, exalted is He: ﴿On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks, none shall speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and who speaks what is right.﴾

That is because the angels are the greatest of created beings in rank and standing, and the most powerful and exalted in station. So He made clear that they do not speak on the Day of Resurrection, out of glorification of their Lord, fear of Him, and submission to Him. How then will the condition of others be?

There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: whoever holds that the angel is superior to the human being may take hold of this verse. This is because the purpose of the verse is that the angels, though they remain fearful, submissive, awestruck and bewildered in the station of God's majesty and the manifestation of His might and greatness, how then will the condition of others be? It is well known that this argument is complete only if they are the noblest of created beings.

The second issue: they differed concerning "the Spirit" in this verse. From Ibn Mas'ud it is reported that it is an angel greater than the heavens and the mountains. From Ibn 'Abbas it is reported that it is an angel among the greatest of the angels in creation. From Mujahid: a creation in the form of the sons of Adam, who eat and drink, and they are not human. From al-Hasan and Qatadah: they are the sons of Adam, and on this view its meaning is "the one possessing a spirit." From Ibn 'Abbas also: the spirits of people. From al-Dahhak and al-Sha'bi: it is Jibril (peace be upon him). This view is the one preferred by al-Qadi (al-Qadi al-Baydawi), who said: because the Qur'an indicates that this name is the name of Jibril (peace be upon him), and it is established that standing is valid for Jibril and speech is valid from him, and it is valid that he be permitted. So how is this name to be diverted from him to a creation we do not know, or to the Qur'an, which cannot validly be described as standing?

As for His saying "ṣaffan" (in ranks): it may be that the meaning is that the Spirit, according to the difference we have mentioned, and all the angels stand in one rank. It is also possible that the meaning is that they stand in two ranks, or in multiple ranks. The word "ṣaff" is originally a verbal noun, and it applies to both the singular and the plural. The apparent sense of the words of the commentators is that they stand in two ranks: the Spirit stands alone in one rank, and all the angels stand in one rank, so that the greatness of his creation is like their ranks. Some said: rather they stand in rows, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]

The third issue: to what does the exception return? There are two views:

One: it returns to the Spirit and the angels. On this reading, the verse indicates that the Spirit and the angels do not speak except when two conditions are met. The first: that God, exalted is He, gives permission. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. The meaning is that they do not speak except by the permission of God.
The second condition: that they say what is right. If it is said: once the Most Merciful has permitted them in that speech, they know that the speech is right without doubt, so what is the benefit in His saying: ﴿and who speaks what is right﴾? The answer is in two respects. The first: the Most Merciful permitted them to speak in general, and then, when that permission is given, they do not speak except what is right. It is as if it were said: they do not utter anything until permission to speak has come, and then, after that permission has come, they strive and speak only words they know to be true and right. This is an intensification in describing them as obedient and devoted. The second respect: its implied sense is: they do not speak except on behalf of ﴿one whom the Most Merciful permits and who speaks what is right﴾, meaning they do not intercede except on behalf of a person whom the Most Merciful has permitted to intercede, and that person was one who spoke what is right. The proponent of this interpretation used this verse to argue that they intercede for the sinners, because they spoke what is right, which is the testimony that there is no god but God. For His saying "and spoke what is right" is satisfied, in its truth, by his having spoken even one right word; how much more so for the person who spoke the word that is the most right of words and spoke the speech that is the most noble of utterances?

Two: the exception does not return to the angels alone, but to all the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. The view that is first stated is preferable, because the return of a pronoun to the nearest referent is preferable.

Know that when God, exalted is He, had established the states of the accountable in the degrees of reward and punishment, and had established the greatness of the Day of Resurrection, He said after it:

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 78, verses 39–40:**

God Most High says: ﴿That is the True Day﴾. "That" points back to what was previously mentioned. There are several aspects to describing the Day as "true":

(First) It contains all truth, and every falsehood is annihilated in it. Since it is perfect in this sense, it is called true, as one says, "So-and-so is all good" when he is described as having much good in him. His saying ﴿That is the True Day﴾ indicates that it is the true day and that everything else is false, because the days of this world have more falsehood than truth.

(Second) The true (al-haqq) is that which is firm and existent. In this sense God is called true, meaning He is firm and it is not permissible for Him to perish. The Day of Resurrection is likewise, so it is true.

(Third) That Day is the one deserving of being called a "day," because in it the hidden things are tested and the inner thoughts are laid bare. As for the days of this world, the states of creation in them are concealed, and their conditions are not known.

God Most High says: ﴿So whoever wills takes a return (ma'ab) to his Lord﴾. Ma'ab means a place of return. The Mu'tazilites (al-Mu'tazila) used this verse as proof of free choice and volition, while our companions (the Ash'arites) related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the meaning is, "So whoever God wills good for, He guides him until he takes a return to his Lord."

Then God, Exalted, increased the warning to the disbelievers, saying: ﴿Indeed We have warned you of a near punishment﴾, meaning the punishment in the Hereafter. Everything that is to come is near. This is like His saying: ﴿As if on the day they see it, they had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾. He called it a warning because by this description He has warned of it in the utmost degree, and that is the meaning of warning.

* * *

Then God, Exalted, said: ﴿The Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾. In this there are several issues:

**Issue one:** The "mā" in His saying ﴿what his hands have sent forth﴾ has two possibilities:

(The first) It is interrogative and object of "sent forth" (qaddamat), meaning: he looks at whatever his hands have sent forth.

(The second) It is in the sense of "that which" (alladhī) and is object of "looks" (yanẓuru). The construction would be: he looks at that which his hands have sent forth. However, on this construction two elisions occur:

(One) He did not say "qaddamat-hu" (sent it forth), but said "qaddamat," so he omitted the returning pronoun.

(Two) He did not say "looks at what they have sent forth" (yanẓuru ilā mā qaddamat), but said "looks what they have sent forth." One says "naẓartu-hu" in the sense of "naẓartu ilayhi" (I looked at him).

**Issue two:** In the verse there are three opinions:

(The first), which is the most apparent, is that "the man" (al-mar') is general, applying to everyone, because the one who is accountable, if he has sent forth the deeds of the righteous, then he has nothing but the great reward, and if he has sent forth the deeds of the disbelievers, then he has nothing but the punishment which God Most High described. There is no hope for any of the accountable who arrive at the Resurrection in anything other than these two. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿The Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾. So blessed is he if he has sent forth the deeds of the righteous, and woe to him if he has sent forth the deeds of the wicked.

(The second opinion), which is the saying of 'Ata', is that "the man" here is the disbeliever, because the believer, just as he looks at what his hands have sent forth, also looks at God's pardon and mercy. As for the disbeliever, who sees nothing but punishment, he sees only what his hands have sent forth, because what reaches him of punishment is nothing but the evil of his own dealings.

(The third opinion), which is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatada, is that "the man" here is the believer. They argued for this with two points:

(The first) God said after this verse: ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust"﴾. Since this is a description of the state of the disbeliever, it must be that the first is a description of the state of the believer.

(The second) The believer, having sent forth good and evil, is in the hand of God Most High between fear and hope, so he waits to see how the matter will turn out. As for the disbeliever, he is certain of punishment, so he has no waiting as to how the matter will turn out, for with certainty there is no waiting.

**Issue three:** Those who hold that good necessitates reward and evil necessitates punishment held fast to this verse, saying: "If the matter were not so, then a man's looking at reward and punishment would not be on account of his deed but on account of something else." The reply to this is that deeds do necessitate reward and punishment, but by the ruling of promise and appointment, not by the ruling of essence.

As for His saying ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust"﴾, there are several interpretations:

(First) On the Day of Resurrection a man looks at what his hands have sent forth. As for the believer, he finds faith and pardon for the rest of his sins, as He said: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 48]. As for the disbeliever, he does not expect pardon, as He said: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with﴾. At that point the disbeliever says: ﴿Would that I were dust﴾, meaning: would that I had not been a living accountable being.

(Second) That he was dust before the resurrection. The meaning according to this is: "Would that I had not been raised for the reckoning, and had remained as I was, dust," like His saying: ﴿Would that it had been the decisive end﴾ [al-Haqqah: 27], and His saying: ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them﴾ [an-Nisa': 42].

(Third) That the animals are gathered, and retribution is made for the hornless (sheep) against the horned, and then it is said to them after the reckoning, "Be dust." At that point the disbeliever wishes that he were like those animals in becoming dust and escaping God's punishment. Some of the Mu'tazilites denied this and said: "When God restores them, they are either recompensed or granted favor. If that is the case, it is not permissible to cut them off from benefits, for that would be a harm to them, and such a thing is not permissible in the Hereafter." Then these (scholars) said: when the term of their recompense ends, God makes every one of them that was of beautiful form a reward for the people of Paradise, and every one that was of ugly form a punishment for the people of Hell. The Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: "It is also not impossible, when God has fulfilled their recompense while they lack full intellect, that God should end their life in a way that they feel no pain, so this is not a harm."

(Fourth) What some of the Sufis (al-Sufiyya) mentioned: he said, "His saying ﴿Would that I were dust﴾ means: Would that I had been humble in obedience to God and had not been arrogant and rebellious."

(Fifth) The disbeliever is Iblis, who sees Adam and his offspring and their reward, so he wishes that he were the thing he had despised when he said: ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [Sad: 76].

And God knows best His intent and the secrets of His Book. May God bless our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and his family and companions.

(The second) It is in the sense of "that which" (alladhī) and is object of "looks" (yanẓuru). The construction would be: he looks at that which his hands have sent forth. However, on this construction two elisions occur:

(One) He did not say "qaddamat-hu" (sent it forth), but said "qaddamat," so he omitted the returning pronoun.

(Two) He did not say "looks at what they have sent forth" (yanẓuru ilā mā qaddamat), but said "looks what they have sent forth." One says "naẓartu-hu" in the sense of "naẓartu ilayhi" (I looked at him).

**Issue two:** In the verse there are three opinions:

(The first), which is the most apparent, is that "the man" (al-mar') is general, applying to everyone, because the one who is accountable, if he has sent forth the deeds of the righteous, then he has nothing but the great reward, and if he has sent forth the deeds of the disbelievers, then he has nothing but the punishment which God Most High described. There is no hope for any of the accountable who arrive at the Resurrection in anything other than these two. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿The Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth﴾. So blessed is he if he has sent forth the deeds of the righteous, and woe to him if he has sent forth the deeds of the wicked.

(The second opinion), which is the saying of 'Ata', is that "the man" here is the disbeliever, because the believer, just as he looks at what his hands have sent forth, also looks at God's pardon and mercy. As for the disbeliever, who sees nothing but punishment, he sees only what his hands have sent forth, because what reaches him of punishment is nothing but the evil of his own dealings.

(The third opinion), which is the saying of al-Hasan and Qatada, is that "the man" here is the believer. They argued for this with two points:

(The first) God said after this verse: ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust"﴾. Since this is a description of the state of the disbeliever, it must be that the first is a description of the state of the believer.

(The second) The believer, having sent forth good and evil, is in the hand of God Most High between fear and hope, so he waits to see how the matter will turn out. As for the disbeliever, he is certain of punishment, so he has no waiting as to how the matter will turn out, for with certainty there is no waiting.

**Issue three:** Those who hold that good necessitates reward and evil necessitates punishment held fast to this verse, saying: "If the matter were not so, then a man's looking at reward and punishment would not be on account of his deed but on account of something else." The reply to this is that deeds do necessitate reward and punishment, but by the ruling of promise and appointment, not by the ruling of essence.

As for His saying ﴿And the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust"﴾, there are several interpretations:

(First) On the Day of Resurrection a man looks at what his hands have sent forth. As for the believer, he finds faith and pardon for the rest of his sins, as He said: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 48]. As for the disbeliever, he does not expect pardon, as He said: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that He be associated with﴾. At that point the disbeliever says: ﴿Would that I were dust﴾, meaning: would that I had not been a living accountable being.

(Second) That he was dust before the resurrection. The meaning according to this is: "Would that I had not been raised for the reckoning, and had remained as I was, dust," like His saying: ﴿Would that it had been the decisive end﴾ [al-Haqqah: 27], and His saying: ﴿On that Day those who disbelieved and disobeyed the Messenger will wish that the earth were leveled over them﴾ [an-Nisa': 42].

(Third) That the animals are gathered, and retribution is made for the hornless (sheep) against the horned, and then it is said to them after the reckoning, "Be dust." At that point the disbeliever wishes that he were like those animals in becoming dust and escaping God's punishment. Some of the Mu'tazilites denied this and said: "When God restores them, they are either recompensed or granted favor. If that is the case, it is not permissible to cut them off from benefits, for that would be a harm to them, and such a thing is not permissible in the Hereafter." Then these (scholars) said: when the term of their recompense ends, God makes every one of them that was of beautiful form a reward for the people of Paradise, and every one that was of ugly form a punishment for the people of Hell. The Qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: "It is also not impossible, when God has fulfilled their recompense while they lack full intellect, that God should end their life in a way that they feel no pain, so this is not a harm."

(Fourth) What some of the Sufis (al-Sufiyya) mentioned: he said, "His saying ﴿Would that I were dust﴾ means: Would that I had been humble in obedience to God and had not been arrogant and rebellious."

(Fifth) The disbeliever is Iblis, who sees Adam and his offspring and their reward, so he wishes that he were the thing he had despised when he said: ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [Sad: 76].

And God knows best His intent and the secrets of His Book. May God bless our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and his family and companions.
